title: Louise Cowan's Speech on Teachers - Part I
author: Louise Cowan
summary: In this speech for a Learning Center dedication, curated from the Cowan Archive, Louise Cowan distinguishes teachers from other mentors such as parents and coaches. A teacher, she says, has the twofold task of forming the young for their own sake and for society's, preserving and extending the heritage of a civilization. Families and neighborhoods are not schools, whose purpose is forming citizens knowledgeable and wise enough to govern themselves. She criticizes a modern philosophy that treats teaching as behavioral training, strips out elevating metaphors and reduces education to facts, skills and incessant testing. Machines can deliver information and skills, but not the principles and virtues a democracy needs. She closes this first part by tracing how the word value replaced virtue, a word meaning strength of character.
points: Cowan separates teachers from ordinary mentors by their lifework of forming the young for their own sake and for society's.
The purpose of teaching is to preserve and extend the heritage of a civilization, passing on what is culturally valuable.
Schools differ from families and neighborhoods in aiming at citizens knowledgeable and wise enough to govern themselves.
Modern education has become literal, fact- and skill-centered and test-driven, losing the elevating metaphors that reveal nobility.
She argues that replacing the word virtue with value weakened the public virtues a free society requires.
quotes: Teachers are instructing the young then not primarily to enable their charges to succeed in life but to preserve and extend the heritage of a civilization—to pass on what is culturally valuable.
Families and neighborhoods are not schools, which have a unique intent and purpose—the formation of citizens who are knowledgeable enough—and wise enough—to govern themselves.

We have tended to make the teaching process sound more like behavioral instruction (something like the training of young animals) than the drawing out of noble aspects in rational and imaginative beings.
We’ve taken away the elevating metaphors from our education—those bundles of symbolic content that have a kind of magical power to reveal a nobility that would otherwise remain hidden.

A teacher is not really needed for the mastery of facts and skills; to gain this sort of information something simply has to capture student attention long enough for bits of data to sink in—or for practice to make perfect.

For facts are mere information, and skills are mere habits of behavior, and neither is necessarily related to principles and virtues needing to be instilled in our young if our democracy is to survive.
Sometime back in the 20th century, which now seems like another epoch completely, we started substituting the word “value” for the older word “virtue.
